PlayStation quietly discontinuing PSVR 2 could cement it as one of the biggest fumbles in gaming hardware history

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This week, PlayStation has removed PSVR 2 from its own virtual stores in the US and in Japan, which follows on from months of stock shortages in the US and UK for the VR headset. The news also comes just a month after it was found that Sony has sold all of its mixed-reality patents to one of its biggest rivals in the space, Meta.

Just three years on from its arrival, the headset seems to be reaching the end of its supported life. Sony's second headset received countless glowing reviews from critics and fans, but its lack of support has led it to an even shorter lifespan than the first PSVR.

To be completely clear, there's been no official word from Sony about it discontinuing PSVR 2, but even for an optimist and massive VR apologist like me, the writing's on the wall.

Immediate reception from fans was cold because of PSVR 2's launch price. Its lack of support for PC until halfway through its life almost certainly cut it off from a big chunk of this comparably small gaming market. A price drop definitely restored some good faith, but by the time it arrived, Sony had already made its lack of support on the games side a big red flag.

Since reviewing PSVR 2, I've held the strong belief that this is the best option for gaming that people can buy - even after testing newer rivals. Meta has produced affordable, mixed-reality excellence with the Quest 3 headsets. Pimax and HTC have proven visually lossless will always be unmatched, but PSVR 2's all round features, its jaw-dropping displays, and its gaming-centric design have always given it an edge I haven't found elsewhere on the shelves.

Sony made something that, although had a lofty price tag, was far beyond the competition in terms of its specs, features, and user experience. It knew from its first VR rodeo, and countless game console generations, that dedicated software support is the name of the game, and yet, it chose to sit idly by and let the idea of PSVR 2 gather dust just as the headset itself did on people's shelves.

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

If you ask a lot of gamers, the fate of PSVR 2 was sealed long before its gradual withdrawal from stores. In 2024, Sony shuttered or repurposed all of the VR studios it had spent so much money to acquire during the PS4 lifecycle. Sony London, the developer of PlayStation VR Worlds, was closed. Firesprite made Horizon Call of the Mountain, but has since seen downsizing. Guerilla Cambridge was closed despite making PSVR's well-received RIGS. Team Asobi made an Astro Bot VR title for PSVR, but it was repurposed for flat-screen Astro titles that admittedly went on to win GOTY.

Even if that was all unavoidable for business reasons I'm not privy to, it didn't need to be the death knell for PSVR 2.

There's plenty that PlayStation could have tried to do to keep interest alive. The VR category on the PlayStation Plus catalog has gotten smaller and smaller by the month. Free games as part of the service almost never included a VR game, which incentivized absolutely none of the PS5's user base to adopt the hardware. A lack of VR games in the wider market is a larger chicken-and-egg problem at the moment, but there are plenty on SteamVR that PlayStation could have made a bigger deal of securing.

Despite even the first PSVR headset having a multitude of bundles and demos to support its sales on the shelves, PSVR 2 still only has one: the Horizon Call of the Mountain bundle it launched alongside.

State of Plays have made it clear that VR is no longer a priority to the PlayStation ecosystem for people who spent their hard-earned cash on a VR headset. The last time a VR game featured was back in the middle of 2025 when Thief VR: Legacy of Shadow was announced.

While I find it difficult to fault the design of PSVR 2, I can't condone its lack of a PC lifeline, namely, any anticipatory support for PC when it launched.

In the end, the lack of an intuitive linking system to PC cut the legs out from under PSVR 2 from the first. The PC adaptor was such a welcome addition that gave the headset a bit more momentum, but almost every review from customers and critics found it was clunky, complicated, and a very imperfect fix for a device that should have been able to link to a PC much more simply.

A $50 add-on that went out of stock almost immediately and was then imitated by unlicensed third-party brands was not the most appealing to begin with, but the fact that even when it worked, foveated rendering and headband haptic feedback didn't carry over from PS5 probably didn't add much appeal.

Fair enough, today, PlayStation has pulled back from any and all PC support, but back in 2023 its experiment with PC hardware and software releases was in full swing. It seems both incredibly arrogant and even more short-sighted of the folks at Sony not to make such a pricey bit of hardware compatible with the biggest segment of the VR market. A DisplayPort or HDMI port on the headset, or even a natural Windows USB connection from the get-go that lined up with Sony's Inzone hardware, could have given PSVR 2 a failsafe if the PS5 player base didn't adopt it.

Sony's mishandling of what is still a top-class bit of hardware will puzzle me for years to come. Like I say, I'm a massive VR fan, so my biases are clear, but I believe PSVR 2 could have survived a lack of support on the software side, or a lack of wider (and easier) PC support.

It didn't stand a chance against both of those things at once.

If you're interested in buying a different VR headset, check out our review of the Steam Frame, the Meta Quest 3, or the Pimax Dream Air.

#3771. One World of Warcraft: Forever player is working on a first-person mod that's a love letter to retro RPGs like Hexen and Morrowind

One World of Warcraft: Forever player is attempting to turn Blizzard's new MMO endeavour into a Morrowind-esque first-person fantasy RPG, full of retro animations harkening back to the good ol' days. And there's no generative AI in sight.

The project, known as Retro Forever, is the work of modder Arhkain, who's so far published two dev vlogs detailing the nature of his work. He opens the first vlog by describing how he always wanted to view the world of Azeroth through his character's eyes, but was met with a lack of adequate options to support this style of play. That encouraged him to find his own solutions, which is how Retro Forever was born.

The result is a WoW Forever mod aiming to incorporate "fully immersive" first-person graphics - whether it be for combat, cooking, or flying across the world - with a presentation style reminiscent of classic first-person fantasy games like Morrowind or Hexen. In fact, the mod currently uses assets pulled and modified from those games.

Retro Forever - which is described as a "clever combination of addons that already exist" - includes a custom user interface, as well as animations attached to specific spells and abilities. That means, if you're a mage and attack an enemy with a spell, you'll see a custom animation of your character doing that spell.

The bad news is the mod isn't publicly available right now, and currently only works with a selection of mage spells and other class abilities. However, that's set to expand - and Arhkain recently revealed an artist has expressed interest in joining the project for original asset creation.

As for the no-generative AI deal, Arhkain said the tool "wouldn't help" in the mod's development. And when Retro Forever has been updated with original art to replace its currently borrowed assets, it should also dodge any legal pitfalls too. Nice!

The Air Power G10 is interesting in a few ways. First, it has three 120 mm fans pre-installed at the front that are able to swivel up and down. They come with dust filters too, which is a nice touch. These are daisy-chained around the back of the case, which means you can simply connect these to the rear fan and bottom fan (all of which are included in the box), then into your motherboard.

You can take the front, top, and sides off the G10 without any tools; with tools, you can take off the PSU shroud and swap it with the bracer on the bottom for the rear fans. This is a relatively niche bit of customisation, but should you need to swap around the PSU position or want your fans pointing directly under the graphics cards, it's pretty simple to do so.

Formula V provides the 3D design files for the front panel. With these, you can design and attach your own panels and fan braces. I like a lot of the decisions made with the Air Power G10, and building a PC in it is not only easy but even rather fun thanks to a decent amount of open space and convenient access.

If you have the right PSU, installation in the Air Power G10 is super easy. That’s a pretty big if, though. In the box, you get three front fans preinstalled and daisy-chained. You also get a back fan pre-installed, then one bottom fan, which is not installed. Simply connect the three back fans to the front fan and the bottom fan, then plug them into your motherboard, and you are good to go.

The case only supports PSUs up to 160 mm in length, which means many power supplies we had on hand simply would not fit in it. I tried with the Be Quiet! Dark Power 12, and Dark Power Pro, as well as the Cooler Master V1000. These three are bigger than the 160 mm Formula V advertises the Air Power G10 can fit, but it means you can't just grab any old PSU and throw it in. I had to shrink down to the Corsair SF600, a small-form-factor power supply, to get it hooked up with what we had in the office.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

You can take off the shroud above it, but that only gives the PSU some unnecessary headroom; it doesn't give much more length. And an exact 160 mm or less is a pretty tight squeeze, especially when you consider some PSU cables can be rather chunky and might have to be pressed against the side of the case for prolonged periods of time.

The case comes with a neat power cable that hooks from the back of the case underneath the rear fans, and then near the front to get to the PSU. This means your power cable will be colour-coded with your rig, but it also means you have to swap the PSU section and bottom fan shroud if your PSU power port is on the wrong side. You can take out this cable, but it leaves a big gap at the back of the case, which cheapens the clean aesthetic of the build.

Given you can open up the case from almost every angle but the back without any tools, I found myself only using the screwdriver in very select cases, like fastening the motherboard and kitting the AMD stock CPU cooler. You do need a screwdriver, but only sparingly, which also means having to keep track of fewer screws as you build.

PSU problems out of the way, the G10 has plenty of empty space in the back for cable management, and there are a couple of ties in the box once you're happy with it all. I'm no cable management pro, but I managed to get it looking tidy enough in a short amount of time. A big benefit of the three front fans being preinstalled is that they're relatively plug-and-play.

Aesthetics are the name of the game with the white model I got my hands on, especially when you consider it fetches $10 more than some of its non-white counterparts. And for that, it does look pretty sweet. The white steel is only ever disrupted by the silver of the screws, and they look tidy in application too. The top even has a small leather-like handle.

It is a lovely-looking case that looks even better when all the fans are spinning (assuming you daisy-chained it correctly).

I didn't even commit to an all-white build, and still found myself casually staring into its pretty spinning fans on more than one occasion. I even quite like the three-fan front panel, and its RGB lighting. It's sunken into the front panel, but sleek enough to look quite clean. The Air Power G10 manages to look like its own unique case without getting ugly in the process, which is an impressive feat.

Recorded with only the case fans that come with the G10 and a stock AMD CPU cooler

The rig I built was kitted with an AMD Ryzen 5 7600X, an XFX Swift AMD Radeon RX 9060 XT, 32 GB of memory, and two SSDs. Thanks to it being a large case and coming fitted with five 120 mm fans, the Air Power G10 has some rather solid temps. In a whole suite of gaming tests, the 9060 XT only ever got to a maximum of 64.8 °C and an average of 57 °C.

The CPU, on the other hand, got up to a max temperature of 91 °C, with an average of 81 °C. That's pretty high, but not the fault of the case. I stuck a simple stock AMD cooler on the CPU, and a 360 mm cooler up top would keep those CPU temps down. Still, airflow is solid in the case with the fans set to the positions Formula V intends (three on the front, one in the rear and one on the bottom).

Though I noticed a shift of about a degree on average when pushing the front fans up or down, that's well within the standard deviation, so I'd say it makes little to no difference which way you point them. You could perhaps get slightly better cooling out of a specific angle when you place the PC near a breeze or on the other side of a fan, but I'd recommend making your rig as uncomplicated as possible.

I also noticed the GPU temperature going up ever so slightly when pointing the bottom fan back towards the PSU, which is, again, within a standard deviation.

$100 for the white variant pushes the Power G10 just out of budget and instead into 'slightly above budget' in my book. The Corsair 3200D is $30 less, supports PSUs up to 180 mm (though it has a slightly smaller GPU space), and it even comes in white too. It only comes with three Corsair RS120 fans, but for that $30 difference, you could pick up a five-pack of Arctic P12 Pro to add to the party. They're not hard to pick up for cheap on Newegg or Amazon either.

For $20 more, you can pick up the excellent Phanteks XT View Matrix (which also comes in white), and this one also comes with three pre-installed 120 mm fans. This is all to say there isn't a shortage of sweet white cases.

The Air Power G10 is certainly unique enough in the looks and modularity department to intrigue me, but it's not cheap enough that it's automatically worth a punt with its flaws, and It's no longer super difficult to get a pretty white case for cheap.

4. Best budget compact: Thermaltake S100 TG Snow Edition

The Formula V Air Power G10 really does offer solid airflow without having to bring your own fans, and it looks good in the process whilst being easy to build into. But a pretty small PSU size limit and a pricier white model let it down.

James is a more recent PC gaming convert, often admiring graphics cards, cases, and motherboards from afar. It was not until 2019, after just finishing a degree in law and media, that they decided to throw out the last few years of education, build their PC, and start writing about gaming instead. In that time, he has covered the latest doodads, contraptions, and gismos, and loved every second of it. Hey, it’s better than writing case briefs.

It's still early days for Warner Bros' new DC universe headed James Gunn and Peter Safran, but we just got one exciting update on one of the upcoming DC movies on the way. Dynamic Duo will officially star Mason Thames as Dick Grayson/Robin. It's perfect casting, especially since the actor once told us himself how much the character means to him.

In a new interview with Collider, Safran confirmed Thames casting, which has been rumored for awhile. Here's what he said about the 19-year-old from How To Train Your Dragon and The Black Phone movies earning the role.

We always talk about wanting volunteers and not recruits to be part of the DCU, to be part of DC Studios, and Mason always wanted to be Dick Grayson. He just did. And he came in, and auditioned the shit out of it, and was awesome. He's a wonderful young actor, but boy, did he want this. He was just obsessed. When he came over to the DC offices, he came over with his dad at the time, and we’ve got tons of great archives and stuff in there, and wanted to take a picture of everything and with everything. He's a fan.

When Mason Thames stopped by San Diego Comic-Con's suite back in July, he gushed with us about his deep love for the character. As he shared with us at the time:

I'm a big comic book nerd... Spider-Man's always been No. 1, but I love Robin, specifically Dick Grayson's Robin. I've loved his comic books. I have about a million of them. It's just fun to see his journey from him being first Robin to becoming Nightwing, to becoming kind of the symbol of what Batman wishes Batman was. And, he's always kind of been the best of him.

This new role for Mason Thames is absolutely deserved because he truly knows his stuff. In between chatting with him, I could see how genuinely stoked he was to be at his first San Diego Comic Con. He was asking me about all the tips to best enjoy the experience, and was hyped to walk the floor and get the full SDCC experience. He really and truly is one of us. Here's the video:

A post shared by CinemaBlend (@cinemablend)

DC's Dynamic Duo movie is set to have Thames' Dick Grayson working together with another Robin iteration, Jason Todd. Grayson grew up in a family of circus performers, but had to watch his parents fall to their deaths while trying to be complete one trick (after the act was sabotaged). He becomes Batman's first sidekick. Jason Todd, on the other hand, is a character who grew up on the streets of Gotham to a petty thief and a drug addict for parents before being taken in by Batman.

When the movie was announced it on X in October 2024, Gunn revealed it'd be "a mix of animation, puppetry, and CGI," making it a rather unique take on the characters. While Thames is presumably just taking on the voice role for Robin in this movie, Gunn has previously said this in 2023, per IGN:

And what we're doing with the DCU is we are having animation tied directly into live-action television and movies and games all intertwined within the same universe. We're going to cast actors that are going to be able to play the characters in this as well as in other things.

While we should keep in mind these comments are on the older side, Mason Thames looks absolutely ready to play Robin as is in live-action. And, I hope Dynamic Duo is the start of a long journey of the actor playing the role across a variety of mediums.

It's also worth nothing the movie is also produced by Matt Reeves, who's been the filmmaker behind The Batman films with Robert Pattinson. I wonder if we could see a version of his Dick Grayson in his universe? Dynamic Duo is set to hit theaters on September 22, 2028 following the release of Man of Tomorrow and The Batman: Part II next year. Congrats to Mason Thames on manifesting a dream role of his!

#3767. COD Modern Warfare 4 has seemingly answered DMZ players' PvE calls with new Story Mission changes - but there are major caveats

For as long as Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ extraction mode has been available, there've been calls for PvE-only servers. Developer Infinity Ward, for its part, has maintained the mode is designed as a PvPvE experience, but it's now seemingly made a change offering solo players something of a compromise, albeit with caveats.

In DMZ, your choice of deployment type dictates the matchmaking pool you're put into. You can choose to freely roam the map, picking up tasks as you go, or participate in slightly more structured Dynamic Ops which constantly generate tasks for you to do. But DMZ also has Story Missions, a title that suggests they're private instances. But that wasn't the case at launch. Although the number of players allowed into Story Mission instances appeared to be smaller than in other modes, it was still possible to run into other players, which meant potentially unwanted PvP encounters.

Now, however, Infinity Ward appears to have made Story Missions private, but only for solo players, and only when playing a Story Mission for the first time - after which, repeated attempts will be much less forgiving.

Infinity Ward has not officially announced a change, but players began noticing it on Reddit and elsewhere, and I wanted to investigate for myself: I just finished a Story Mission - a first attempt - and despite making as much noise as possible, I ran into no other players. The Recent Players list in the social tab, which displays the names of players you've recently crossed paths with, was likewise empty for me. I also noticed zero activated UAV Towers and SAM Sites - a rare sight in PvPvE matches where players always run to the former to reveal enemies around them. There's some suggestion you may still run into others in a Story Mission, however, so best not lower your guard. As welcome as the change is, it highlights the split in DMZ's community. Many would rather not cross paths with other players, and it's especially frustrating for those expecting a purely PvE mode in this year's Call of Duty.

#3766. How to collect Nami’s Tangerines to help Sanji protect them in Fortnite Treasure Hunters

Fortnite’s Treasure Hunters season has quite a few different One Piece-themed missions available for you to tackle. One of the first ones you’ll encounter tasks you with collecting Nami’s Tangerines to help Sanji protect them.

The loot pool is massive, so figuring out how to find any specific item around the island can be tricky. If this task is giving you trouble, here’s how to collect Nami’s Tangerines to help Sanji protect them in Fortnite.

Nami’s Tangerines are a random loot drop item you can find just about anywhere on the island while looting. There is no specific, guaranteed way to find them, which means you instead have to regularly loot and hope you eventually come across them.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

You have a chance of finding Nami’s Tangerines when opening any loot container you come across while exploring. This includes:

You can also find Nami’s Tangerines sitting on the ground anywhere around the island. They’re fairly common, so once you’re actively looking for them, finding the total amount required for this mission should be fairly easy.

Each time you come across Nami’s Tangerines, you’ll generally find more than one. Typically, they come in bundles of around three. This helps you progress through the mission associated with them much faster, as you need to find quite a few of them to get it done.

To complete the collect Nami’s Tangerines to help Sanji protect them quest, you need to find a total of 16 Nami’s Tangerines around the island. You don’t actually have to eat them; instead, you simply need to pick them up and have them in your inventory briefly for them to count toward this task.

You can find all 16 Nami’s Tangerines in one match or instead slowly work your way through this task across a few different ones. All that matters for this mission is that you eventually do manage to collect a total of 16 at some point before the season ends.

There are plenty of other missions you can find and work through around the island after checking this one off. If you’re unsure what to do next, you might consider contacting Slone on the Slone Phone in Plunder Port, collecting a map fragment at The $.$. Rocky, using Sprite Wanted Posters to dig up and open Sprite Chests, and unlocking Solid Gold A$AP Rocky.

I've been hands-on with the book for a few days, and it's looking good so far

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're not careful, a project like D&D World of Warcraft can be a poisoned chalice. It'd be easy to fall into the trap of just rehashing the MMO that inspired it, key-jangling your audience with nostalgic-yet-empty references that ultimately ring hollow. In much the same way, the two franchises share enough DNA to be siblings – finding something new and not retreading old ground in one of the best tabletop RPGs is easier said than done.

After a few days rifling through this book, though, I'd say it's clear that the team at Wizards of the Coast have been able to thread that needle. D&D World of Warcraft manages to serve both its audiences well with compelling new challenges for one and a meaningful opportunity to explore beyond the edge of the MMO map for another. There's obviously room to improve and expand here, just like the video game it's based on. However, first impressions suggest this is sweet wine rather than toxin.

The physical version of D&D World of Warcraft is currently up for pre-order ahead of a November 17 release date, but if you have a Master Tier subscription at D&D Beyond, you can access the digital file right now.

While it's appealing enough to galavant across Azeroth on tabletop (with each continent and conflict detailed in a busy worldbuilding chapter), let's be honest: one of the real draws for this book is its classes. A grand total of 13 are introduced in the first chapter, and they act as subclasses for D&D's core class list. While many are reskinned or edited versions of existing Dungeons & Dragons builds, a few are entirely new. By and large, they work well – but from what I've seen, it's a sliding scale.

First, the good. Some really do add a compelling, shiny new toy for us to play with, and chief amongst these are the three 'Hero' classes: Death Knight, Demon Hunter, and Evoker. The implacable Death Knight got an "oh, damn" out of me as we progressed from powerful Runeforging and ghostly steeds that can pass through foes to deadly spells that will make your allies very grateful you're on their side. Meanwhile, the Demon Hunter is a force to be reckoned with long before you consider Soul Fragments that let you regain health and damage foes in one fell swoop… or start double-jumping like goddamn Super Mario.

While these Hero classes are only available from level 3 (which makes sense in-universe, what with them representing the best of the best), they're appealing no matter whether you're coming at this as a D&D player wanting something new or a WoW veteran hoping to recreate their favorite character.

At the other end of the scale are classes that feel a bit too similar to their D&D equivalent. Despite some revolving around specializations that help them avoid being lost in the shuffle (like the Hunter's emphasis on pets, the Monk's focus on Mystic Brews, or Druid's beast forms with bespoke powers), it's more an extension of something we already have rather than a completely novel approach. The Warrior is particularly thin, with just a few new Battle Master maneuvers beyond what D&D Fighters normally get.

That's not a huge problem, of course, and I may change my tune once I've dug into them some more. Nonetheless, I have a feeling some of these classes will shine brighter than others.

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

This book does its level best to make everyone feel welcome, but a word of warning to total Dungeons & Dragons beginners – if you're hoping to play, you will need the free basic rules at D&D Beyond or a Player's Handbook (currently $39.99 at Amazon) to run D&D World of Warcraft. As for prospective Dungeon Masters who are hoping to lead sessions for their friends, you'll need both the Player's Handbook and the Monster Manual (also $39.99 at Amazon). The Dungeon Master's Guide ($49.97 at Amazon) would be helpful too, but I think you could probably get away without it.

The main reason many of us will rock up on D&D World of Warcraft's shores are the dungeons, though, and I'm happy to report these deliver the goods.

Squirrelled away in the back half of the book are six dungeons, all drawn from across WoW history – from Shadowfang Keep to Onyxia's Lair. All of them weigh in at around six-to-eight pages each, and every one is stuffed to the gunwales with encounters, plot hooks, and bosses that should give most parties plenty to chew on. Alongside fierce encounters fans will be happy to see again, there are plenty of fun complications to spice up standard combat (like sabotaging the pirate ship Juggernaut in Deadmines or enduring waves of foes while ritual braziers light your way to the final boss of Blackfathom Deeps).

Crucially, they don't just have to be a gauntlet of fights; you're encouraged to allow any and all plans to complete the mission, be it stealthy disguises or some other cunning plot that can only be achieved with the imagination in D&D. This – and the inclusion of random encounter tables – help avoid these dungeons feeling like simple retreads.

Just be aware that none of them are blow-by-blow guides on how to run each dungeon. Much like other releases for D&D's revised Fifth Edition, the broad strokes are spelled out but you're left to fill in the gaps yourself. This is fine if you're an experienced Dungeon Master who's used to improvising, but may be trickier if you're totally new to this game.

Still, that shouldn't stop you from trying – from what I've seen, the effort is more than worthwhile. Which is just as well; there's a lot riding on D&D World of Warcraft, what with it being the first 'Universes Beyond' crossover ahead of next year's D&D Star Wars project.

If this book is any indication, I'm feeling hopeful about what comes next.

Speaking of D&D Star Wars, it's giving me Andor vibes with promises to let you "fly daring missions" and fight the Empire as a secret Rebel team.

I've been writing about games in one form or another since 2012, but these days you'll find me managing GamesRadar+'s tabletop gaming and toy coverage (I spend my time here handling everything from board game reviews to the latest Lego news). I've also been obsessed with Warhammer since the 1990s, and love nothing more than running tabletop RPGs like D&D as a Dungeon Master.

Disney has always been known for its animated blockbusters, but Frozen (which is streaming with a Disney+ subscription) became a full-blown sensation upon its release in 2013. Its sequel Frozen II crushed at the box office, and two more sequels were quickly announced. Although the studios' Head of Animation recently revealed a big change coming to the next two installments of the franchisee

The first Frozen III footage debuted at D23 over the summer, so anticipation for the threequel is steadily building. While we'll have to wait another year until it arrives in November of 2027, Disney's Jared Bush spoke to Collider about how the studio is approaching the next two movies. He revealed that they're putting a full emphasis on the third movie, rather than trying to put out 3 and 4 in quick succession. In his words:

Looking at Frozen 3 and what a Frozen 4 could look like, I know early on it was, 'We're going to put them right together, and they're going to be out in the world. It's going to happen quick.' That's not what we're doing, for a lot of reasons.

Rather than trying to produce a third and fourth Frozen movie as a cash grab (although they're sure to rake in the bucks), it sounds like the powers that be at Disney are putting story first. This is sure to be a relief for fans who might be worried about the property's legacy being soiled by the next two installments.

Fans are excited for Anna and Kristoff's wedding in the threequel, and to reportedly see Olaf get a love interest. Although we shouldn't expect Frozen III to do a bunch of set up for the developing fourth movie. As Bush went on to say:

To me, an important one is we want to make sure that Frozen 3 is the best movie it can possibly be, so that when you get to the end of the movie, do you feel like you've watched a complete story? That it feels like something that feels fulfilling. That doesn't always mean that everything is buttoned up, but it does mean that you have to be building to something that feels worthy of the end of a franchise that's that important to people.

Honestly, I love this strategy. Rather than getting too big picture about the Frozen franchise as a whole, it sounds like the next two installments will tell independent, fully formed stories. So we shouldn't expect any MCU-esque credits scene that help to set up the fourth movie once Frozen III hits theaters next year.

Sometimes thinking too far ahead can frustrate moviegoers when it comes to franchise films. For instance, Halloween Kills got some backlash upon its release for keeping Jamie Lee Curtis' Laurie Strode in the background and set up her role in the threequel. Luckily the third Frozen movie won't be doing that, and will instead tell its own complete narrative.

All will be revealed when Frozen III hits theaters November 24th, 2027. Since its not on the 2026 movie release list, we'll have to practice patience until footage get its wide release.

#3763. Nintendo tried adding fast travel to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, before devs realised "we were missing out on the moments of discovery"

"I thought we needed to address this in this new version."

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is being wrapped up in all kinds of modern touches for its imminent Nintendo Switch 2 remake (that owl seems to be less chatty, for starters), but there's at least one quality-of-life feature borrowed from Breath of the Wild that the developers felt was better left on the cutting room floor: fast travel.

In Nintendo's latest Ask The Developer blog post, long-time series producer Eiji Aonuma explained that he initially asked the game's remakers to add warp points so players could get around Hyrule without having to spam rolls and presumably make Link violently ill in the process. But he and the team quickly realised fast travel doesn't work so well in a game that's still, in its bones, almost three decades old.

"In The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, there are many warp points that enable players to move quickly around the game's vast world. In the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, you could get around a bit faster by spamming forward roll, so I think a lot of players spent their time doggedly rolling across Hyrule Field whenever they needed to be somewhere in a hurry," Aonuma said.

"I thought we needed to address this in this new version. So I asked the team to add warp points that didn't exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts. But when we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, 'Wait, what's this?' Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren't working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again."

There you have it. No fast-travel points in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake, and it sounds like it's for the best. I avoided warping around Breath of the Wild's open world for the same reasons Aonuma laid out - spotting something odd way in the distance, slowly finding a way to reach it, and then discovering a funky little Korok seed was always a thrill that wouldn't have been possible by cutting out the trek in between main objectives.

Talking about why Nintendo chose to revive Ocarina of Time now, Aonuma said some of the younger developers on the team had maybe never played the original game 28 years ago, and remaking it could "trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development."

As for the remake's somewhat divisive art style, art director Aya Shida said the team "used phrases like 'a puppet-show feel' and 'the analog feel of practical effects films'" early on in production. "Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds," Shida continued.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time comes out on the 5th of November. After getting some hands-on time with the revival, Lottie thought it was shaping up to be a brilliant remake.

#3762. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake review – Remasterpiece

An all-time classic reborn respectfully and beautifully.

I’ve talked in the past about how I’m not particularly a fan of the Zelda games, but it’s mostly because I’ve just never really dived into them, especially the latest open-world ones. But for Ocarina of Time, I’ve dabbled many times before and always respected it for how much it’s loved, even if I never could quite grasp the excitement myself.

As a kid, I remembered feeling overwhelmed and annoyed with the game’s controls (especially on that cumbersome Nintendo 64 controller) and muddy framerate that even then made it feel like a slog. Thankfully, with the newest version for Nintendo Switch 2, all of those issues have been assuaged to create a genuine masterpiece, reborn for modern-day gamers.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is genuinely one of the best games I’ve ever played, and one that I think all players of all ages should experience, whether they’re a hardcore fan of the original or a newcomer going in with zero knowledge. It’s just that good.

It all starts with a boy in the forest, a chosen one of sorts, who is shockingly thrust into an exciting, adorable journey to meet a princess and save the world. From there, from what I’ve gathered, it’s the same timeless story you remember from 1998. I venture to guess that long-time fans of this game will have a very emotional experience reliving it

At its heart, Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 is what I would call a respectful remake/remaster, even if many will probably feel like Nintendo played it a bit too safe this time around. The changes made here have been minimal, focusing on quality-of-life improvements like the game’s controls, visuals, and sound, to enhance the experience without changing it very much at all.

Remakes are always a tricky task, because you need to maintain the allure of the original while also making it worthwhile to play a second time around. There’s been two kinds of remakes in recent years: games like Resident Evil 4 or Final Fantasy VII, which reshape the story and gameplay in numerous ways, or Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater and Demon’s Souls, which stay very true to the original, while focusing more on modernization and quality-of-life. Ocarina of Time definitely falls into the latter.

At the outset, the beauty of modern tech and the Switch 2’s hardware is on full display, boasting some of the best visuals the new console has released yet, especially when it comes to adding details that were not possible on N64: interiors look different thanks to no longer being flat polygons, Link’s tunics have awesome designs in the fabric, and even change color when it gets wet. And then there’s little things, how Link’s mouth subtly opens when taking a breath between notes on the Ocarina (you can also play the songs in the game by humming into your Switch 2, which is just plain cool).

It’s all incredibly detailed and gorgeous, and it’s locked at a rock-solid 60 FPS throughout, creating a smooth experience that we could’ve only ever dreamed of when dealing with the 20-FPS slog the original game offered.

Putting another of my complaints about the original to rest, the controls have been reimagined for modern games and gamers, and are incredibly well optimized for the Switch 2, especially when it comes to the Pro Controller (my preferred method whenever possible). Link can now sprint, and there’s a dedicated button for jumping, making platforming sections a joy. And yes, even the Water Temple is way better now, with the ability to quickly equip and unequip the Iron Boots by pressing down on the D-pad.

The hero can now also target foes with the ZL button and lock onto them when close, making combat a breeze, and maybe even a bit too easy, with nary a real challenge in my 25-plus hours in a first run, even with the game’s awesome and memorable boss fights. I couldn’t help but feel a bit of the adventure’s age here, so it would’ve been cool to see the combat maybe tweaked a bit to bring more of a challenge, but I don’t think it’s a huge deal either way.

This still feels like a masterclass in level design and gradual progression, all these years later. There’s no XP to earn, no checklists, just gradually getting stronger and unlocking new items to help you reach new heights on your journey, with some minor side quests to get into along the way.

Other additions to the adventure for 2026 include Threads of Time, which is a tapestry that weaves Link’s story as you play it, but also serves as a bit of a quest log if you don’t know where to go next. This is very helpful considering there are a ton of side quests, collectibles, and minor interactions to find both in the open world and dungeons you must conquer.

You can easily learn where to go or what to do by talking to NPCs around the vast kingdom of Hyrule, but the tapestry will occasionally update with an objective that you can finish (or not) by gently pushing you in a direction. For me, it was nice to have, considering I don’t remember much about the original game.

There’s also the Hall of Fallen Foes, which is a menagerie of enemies you’ve defeated that you unlock in the later stages of the game. It serves as something of a museum, allowing to to walk around and view the models of monsters and enemies you’ve taken down, but also do battle with them again to reprise the boss fights at your leisure.

The other main difference in this version of the game is the addition of voice acting in certain cutscenes. Many of the game’s conversations are done through text dialogue, but big story beats are voice-acted by a number of important characters like Navi, the Great Deku Tree, Zelda, and of course, Ganon. Everyone here sounds great, which is easy for me to say because I haven’t had my own version of their voices in my head for a few decades like long-time fans will. But don’t worry, the silent protagonist stays silent here, too, other than his classic grunts and exclamations while exerting himself.

The changes made to Ocarina of Time feel meaningful and worthwhile, and they do nothing to detract from the original game’s legendary experience. Instead, they enhance it in every way, making an unforgettable journey more accessible and fun than it ever has been.

I got a little emotional while playing OoT on Switch 2, especially when using the Ocarina to travel to and from the past. How jealous I am of Link’s ability to travel back in time. Like Link, I first entered the Temple of Time as a child and returned as an adult. Much has changed in the 28 years since the original was released, but the charm of this game is still there, and it feels prevalent throughout, even with a “modern” art style and rerecorded musical score.

I will leave a word of warning, however: make multiple saves before heading to the last areas of the game to take on the final boss, if you want to reach 100 percent completion and take on all the game has to offer. There’s no New Game Plus option, and no real option to go back and complete things if you don’t have a separate file ready to go (I’d be happy to find out I missed something if I’m wrong here).

I’d like to close with saying that, in my professional life as a journalist and critic, I’ve always felt hesitant to give out a score like this. It’s not perfect (nothing and no game is), but I’m confident that this is the one game to break that personal barrier with. Ocarina of Time is a legendary experience for a reason, and this remake is one of the best of its kind I’ve played yet. I’m hopeful that longtime fans will enjoy it, and I know that newcomers will find a lot of fun in the franchise if they’re diving in for the first time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dead by Daylight's devs have found themselves in hot water and in the middle of quite a mess. In short, over the Halloween weekend a team member saw TheBurntPeanut playing Dead by Daylight, not in a sponsored stream I may add, and gifted him free DLC, items, and currency.

All the Dead by Daylight DLCs combined come to $335/£301: a substantial sum to just give away to a streamer who makes more money than most of us will see in a lifetime. TheBurntPeanut did then offer to give back all the content and said that he was willing to pay for it, but the official response from an official Dead by Daylight account on his stream was, "We can take the heat. They are yours to keep."

This turned out to be untrue, as shortly after the stream Dead by Daylight rescinded this offer. In an official social media post the devs explained: "we have already removed the content that was granted to the creator".

So what went wrong? Well, gifting hundreds of dollars worth of free stuff to a wealthy content creator who isn't undertaking a sponsored stream isn't a fantastic look. But the DBD community were more annoyed about the conflict in values. Something that the Dead by Daylight creator has now acknowledged:

"When collaborating with a new creator, we normally look thoroughly at their past content to determine whether they are representing the values of inclusion our community expects from us. In this case, this was not taken into proper consideration or discussed as a group.

"When we talk about our values in relation to our community, we mean respect, transparency, diversity, and creating a space where people from different backgrounds and experiences feel welcome. Diversity is one of DBD's core principles and everyone is welcome to play it. But when we choose to work with a creator, we're putting our name next to theirs, and we want to partner with creators whose words and actions share and support that principle."

They have also confirmed that there will be updated request and approval methods for this kind of thing going forward to ensure "any Dead by Daylight spokesperson is properly representing our team and our values."

#3760. The Borderlands series has sold over 100 million copies, and Gearbox is "cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year"

The Borderlands series has sold more than 100m copies across all games, developer Gearbox Software has announced. No surprise, then - the studio also said it's cooking up "big plans" for the evergreen looter shooter's future.

"The Borderlands franchise has officially crossed 100 million units sold," Gearbox boasted in a blog post published today. "There aren't many franchises that have ever hit that milestone, and we certainly didn't get here on our own. For us, it started with that first Borderlands in 2009, and we've been excited about everyone who has joined us in the Borderlands along the way. Borderlands has always had an incredibly passionate community. We've been through a lot together, and your feedback pushes us to make even greater games."

So, where can Vault Hunters expect to go next? Gearbox just finished up on Borderlands 4's Year One roadmap - which included two new playable characters, two Story Packs and more - and it's now "cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year." There's no concrete information about what that looks like for now, but the studio promised Weekly Activity refreshes and Community Challenges will chug on in the meantime.

"We're also taking a bigger look at the franchise as a whole. Where can we take it next? What characters do you want to spend more time with? What stories deserve a payoff? A huge part of that is listening to you," the studio wrote. "All that said, big plans take time, and we need some room to work. You can trust that we'll talk more when the time is right. Now is your chance to influence what we'll say."

Borderlands 4 itself experienced a "softer" than expected launch, thanks partly to the game's wonky PC performance, though it seems to have been a success in the long run. A promised Switch 2 port was also indefinitely delayed earlier in the year. We haven't heard much about that handheld version since, but Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick did say the team were focusing on getting Borderlands 4 into tip-top shape before trying to bring it elsewhere.

In Eurogamer's Borderlands 4 review, Rick Lane said the shooter bought a "more sensible script and a true open world to its pseudo-cel-shaded gun-show, but these moderate improvements are undermined by frustrating exploration and combat that takes too long to properly shine."

Steam just announced changes to its game review process amid an AI flood

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Adding to discussion of Valve's handling of Steam's growing gen AI problem, Epic Games online services product director Alexander Rehm suggests the company's solutions to clone and slop games aren't enough for most people.

Rehm waded into the news on LinkedIn last week, just days before Valve announced a change to Steam's review process in response to a deluge of games evidently fueled, in part, by generative AI. However, this won't necessarily change the outpouring of slop on Steam, as Valve says it doesn't want to dictate what "tools" developers use even if Steam does call for AI disclosures in game store pages. In fact, the idea was to speed up the review process while also enacting new requirements.

At a recent event, Valve business team members affirmed that the company is still working to solve this problem and suggested developers focus on maintaining original, high-quality games that are difficult to clone.

Rehm says this "is a reasonable strategy if you've got the runway and team to do it, and not much use if you're one or two people who shipped a single clever mechanic." This camp, of course, is where a lot of the developers on Steam fall.

The same Valve staff also fielded reports of developers being extorted by AI users who'd threaten to clone a game unless paid off. "Valve also said it hasn't seen reports of developers being extorted over AI clones and that this is a job for law enforcement, not the storefront, which to me reads like a platform that still sees this as someone else's problem," Rehm says.

"If you're building anything indie sized right now, 'keep improving forever' isn't a moat, it's a tax only the well funded can pay," he concludes.

Rehm makes some of the counterarguments that Valve's response initially prompted. How long can Valve kick the can down the road? When will material solutions arrive? How can the creators of hotly anticipated games deal with copycats beating them to launch with identical or near-identical titles? Valve has, as evidenced by its review slowdown, not found the perfect answer, and this process deserves scrutiny.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

The sticking point here is Epic Games' glass house, as some responses to Rehm's post argue. In the replies, you'll find former Valve dev Chet Faliszek, who reckons Epic Games, with its AI-first pivot, once AI-mandatory game jam, and "vibe coded" game launcher, doesn't really have a leg to stand on.

"What an absolutely dishonest read of mixing an off the cuff response in a Q&A with a written statement so you can say they see it as someone else's problem and that they aren't addressing it," Faliszek responds. "I love how you make sure to not to link to either... All the while Tim [Sweeney] screams it is a political act the same as revealing someone's voting record to have an AI disclosure... so explain - how does that work?"

Sweeney has repeatedly criticized Valve for Steam's AI disclosures, which aren't mirrored on the Epic Games Store even though Epic's Fab marketplace does mandate AI disclosures.

"This is a business to business marketplace," Sweeney says of Fab in an October tweet. "Many Fab customers are operating under contracts that require them to understand the providence of all content in their game (including Steam’s own contract that I’ve complained about) and they cannot buy assets without this info."

The CEO has also emphasized the gen AI features of Epic's Unreal Engine 6 – a game-making suite that, one video game lawyer told GamesRadar+, risks legal blowback by ignoring copycat potential.

Separately, Sweeney writes, "What does the law say on the copyright issues associated with training on content? The Anthropic court ruling found they were liable for copyright infringement when torrenting pirated content (as the article quotes me on), but they found that the training itself was fair use. Other courts have found that whether particular content produced by AI was infringing dependent on its similarity to the copyrighted work."

The rush to turn Fortnite into Roblox by way of Unreal Engine integration also calls into question how Epic Games would control a slop flood. Chalmers Robotics Society chairman Maximilian Ygdell tells Rehm, "Epic was fine with using AI trained on others' work, now the same technology is used to empower the people and suddenly it’s an issue? Am I missing something here?"

Epic CEO Tim Sweeney suggests AI could've saved Destiny 2 and will "enable games like Destiny to thrive!"

#3758. How to get Captain X rewards in Fortnite Treasure Hunters

There are many unique skins you can unlock in Fortnite Treasure Hunters. One of the toughest ones to get your hands on is Captain X, a battle pass Outfit that requires quite a bit of progression to obtain.

This style will only be around and available to earn through quests in this season, so if you’re interested in adding it to your collection, you’ve got to get to work on it fast. Since Treasure Hunters is a mini-season, you’ve got quite a limited amount of time to work on it, so here’s how to get Captain X and all of his rewards in Fortnite.

Captain X is the grand prize in the Captain X rewards series, which means you must fully work through this special set of missions to earn him. To progress in this series, you need to complete varying amounts of weekly tasks. A total of 24 weekly quests must be finished to unlock him.

While there are lots of free rewards up for grabs this season, like Solid Gold A$AP Rocky and other rewards in the Pirate Chest, Captain X is not one of them. He is a battle pass-only outfit, which means you must have this pass unlocked to progress toward earning him.

Captain X also cannot be unlocked early on in the season, as there aren’t enough missions available to complete for him. He won’t be obtainable until Nov. 21, close to the very end of Treasure Hunters.

To ensure you’re able to get him, though, you’ll want to keep on top of completing as many weekly quests as possible leading up to his unlock date. Fresh missions are added every week, and checking off as many of them as possible will ensure you’re able to unlock Captain X and all of his associated prizes as soon as it’s possible to do so.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

In total, there are seven rewards available to unlock in the Captain X series. This includes the Captain X Outfit, various key accessory items designed to go with him, and a few other miscellaneous prizes. Here are all of the available Captain X rewards you can get.

There are plenty of quests you can work on to help you get closer to unlocking Captain X. Some missions you may consider tackling next include collecting Nami’s Tangerines to help Sanji protect them, contacting Slone on the Slone Phone in Plunder Port, and using Sprite Wanted Posters to dig up and open Sprite Chests.

#3756. Yakuza creator's new studio and its debut game Gang of Dragon are no more after losing funding from NetEase

Nagoshi Studio has officially shut down and its first game called Gang of Dragon is seemingly no more, months after publisher NetEase pulled funding from the Yakuza-like project.

Toshihiro Nagoshi (often cited as the creator of the brilliant Yakuza and Like A Dragon game series) opened his new studio in 2021 and announced his next game with a very familiar title almost one year ago. Now, the Tokyo-based developer has closed its doors, as confirmed in the Japanese government gazette Kanpo.

The news comes months after employees were told that the studio's future was at risk due to NetEase's funding cuts. Nagoshi Studio reportedly needed another £33.1 million (about $44.4m at the time) to get Gang of Dragon past the finish line - a paycheck NetEase purportedly didn't want to cough up.

The China-based Marvel Rivals and Where Winds Meet publisher has been significantly scaling back on international investments these past few years. Visions of Mana developer Ouka Studios was shut down just after launching its gorgeous action game, Worlds Untold (a studio formed by Mass Effect veteran Mac Walters) had to pause operations to find a new partner, and Halo Infinite lead Jerry Hook's studio also ran into very similar issues last year.

Some developers have been a little luckier. Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture saved itself with a management buyout and now operates as an independent developer, for one.

Not much is known about Gang of Dragon, but its debut trailer featured the violent crime and high drama you'd expect from Nagoshi's previous work. The game also starred Ma Dong-seok, the acclaimed actor you might recognise from films such as Train to Busan and Marvel's Eternals.

There are lots of ways you can customize your experience in Phasmophobia, including an array of ID Cards and Badges you can equip to highlight various achievements and events. Sometimes, these special items are given away to all players, as is the case with the AHA Advocate ID Card and Badge.

ID Cards and Badges are some of the rarest and toughest items to unlock, as many of them require you to sink lots of time into checking off lengthy, complex goals. Because of this, free, easy-to-grab ones are always rather exciting additions you won’t want to miss out on, so here’s how to get the AHA Advocate ID Card and Badge in Phasmophobia.

You can unlock the AHA Advocate ID Card and Badge by logging onto Phasmophobia anytime during the redemption period. This is a free reward granted to all members of the community in celebration of over $200,000 being raised during Phasmophobia’s fundraiser for the American Heart Association Liive.

There are no additional steps you need to take to obtain this item, which is unusual for earning ID Cards and Badges, so it can take a bit of getting used to. Simply boot up the game, visit the board in the lobby, and select the “Accept” option on the AHA Advocate pop-up anytime before Nov. 15 to claim this reward and have it added to your collection forever.

Once you’ve got the AHA ID Card and Badge set unlocked, you can find them under the Customization tab in the lobby. If you’re having trouble finding them, here’s a full breakdown of where to look.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Remember the 3D craze? The Nintendo 3DS, 3D TV, 3D cinema; it was a new, exciting technology that some expected would go mainstream one day. Then the dream just sorta died. People don't talk about it much these days; except for this wonderful project that takes normal videos and turns them, alchemy-like, into slightly more 3D-looking videos using the Steam Frame.

And let me tell you, it's actually pretty good.

It's called framedepth, and it's made by a user going by guix8 on GitHub. It's a plugin for Chrome that adds a stereoscopic 3D effect to any video when viewed via the browser on the Steam Frame.

It's surprisingly fun. I've been watching live gigs and eating challenges on YouTube and the stereoscopic effect is automatically applied once enabled via the extension. It definitely adds some extra level of immersion to it. Not much, but some. I wouldn't go as far to say I felt like I was there in the crowd for either spectacle, and maybe I wouldn't want to be in the firing line of a food challenge, but it's better than I thought it would be. An ever-so-slightly more engaging way to watch YouTube in VR.

The installation process is a bit more involved than your average Chrome plugin, requiring the Steam Frame to be in developer mode. You need to install Chrome on the Steam Frame, which requires a quick trip to the SteamOS desktop to run the Konsole and install via Flathub (flatpak install com.google.Chrome). Then you have to download framedepth from the GitHub and whack more code in the terminal:

cd ~/Downloads && f=$(ls -v framedepth-*-steamos-arm64.tar.gz | tail -1) && echo "$f" # the newest download

sha256sum -c "$f.sha256" && tar -xzf "$f" && cd "${f%.tar.gz}"

bash install.sh # ~/.local/share/framedepth, user service, extension files

Finally, it needs to be loaded as an extension into Chrome, which also requires developer mode to be enabled for extensions in the browser. Once installed, you can enable the 3D effect and change the settings from a dropdown menu right there in Chrome.

The pop-out slider to the max seems to have the most impact on the 3D effect; the equivalent of cranking the 3DS slider all the way up.

There's a bunch to play around with here, but it's worth a go if you have a Steam Frame. If anything, just to rekindle lost excitement for 3D technologies that never managed to win us all over.

#3753. Days Gone studio's next PlayStation exclusive to be revealed and released in 2027, according to new report

Sony's Bend Studio, perhaps one of its lesser discussed development houses, has apparently been deep in development on its next title. The game is reportedly set to be announced in 2027, and released in the same year.

That's according to MP1st, citing "people aware of what's happening at Bend". Like Days Gone, Bend's next game is in third-person. The title is said to include co-op support, but no live service elements.

The report doesn't say whether the game is based on a new IP or an existing one, but it does state that it's not a sequel to Days Gone. The game is apparently "much further along in development" than we realise, which isn't entirely surprising considering Bend has been quiet for years.

The seven years since the release of Days Gone in 2019 have been tumultuous for Bend Studio. The developer revealed in 2022 its next project is a new IP that "builds upon the open-world systems of Days Gone" and includes multiplayer elements.

Two years later, a job post described a game in development at Bend as a triple-A live service project. That unannounced game was then cancelled in 2025, triggering a wave of layoffs at the studio that took place a few months later. Bend hasn't said a word since then.

It's now clear the studio hopped on its next project following the cancellation of that live service game. Seeing as 2026 is nearly over, we're not likely to be waiting much longer to see that mysterious game unveiled.

This weekend Bill Hader is the voice of the animated The Cat In The Hat movie on the 2026 release schedule. But did you know that over a decade ago he totally dressed up as the beloved Dr. Seuss character for a Saturday Night Live sketch? When we chatted with the SNL alum, I had to ask about the memories of playing the role IRL.

Of course, Mike Myers famously took the live-action approach for the 2003 book-to-screen adaptation. In our interview, Hader seems to counts himself lucky to have just lent the voice to the character after spending a day in the literal paws of the character way back when. In his words:

I’m very happy to do it animated because that suit was very hot. And the makeup took a long time. It was the second music number, and then another pre-tape thing that I wasn't in just so they could put all the makeup on me. It was the last sketch of the night, so we did it really fast. So yeah, it was really hot and I had all that stuff on my face. I don't know how Mike Myers did it.

Myers' own process took two and a half hours and was very hot to act in a yak-hair suit all day. Jim Carrey had it even worse as The Grinch. He had to go through such a grueling process a specialist in torture was hired to help him withstand the eight-hour get ready time. In our interview above, you can see Quinta Brunson school Hader on what happened and watch his real-time reaction.

Instead of going through all that makeup time for months, it was just for one night. He played the character on October 11, 2014 in an episode he hosted in the season right after his exit from the show following an eight-year run. You can check out the sketch below:

It’s such a funny spin on the classic children’s book. When two sibling children are bored on a rainy day, they conjure up The Cat in the Hat, but something unexpected happens: he’s already acquainted with their mom, Linda. Playtime with the whimsical figure turns into an awkward reunion between The Cat and Linda. The best line has to be when Linda says: “He’s reliable. I don’t have to say a rhyme to make him come home.” ‘

And then, Linda’s husband ends up being Thing 2, who goes by Jona-Thing now. He comes home disappointed to see The Cat In The Hat with his wife and kids. The sketch hilariously ends with The Cat In The Hat saying “But oh, the places she let me go!” as he leaves them, which is obviously a NSFW reference to another Dr. Seuss book.

When CinemaBlend also spoke to the movie’s writer/directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni, we had to ask if the SNL sketch was involved at all with casting Hader. Here’s what Rivinoja told us:

It was completely random, of course, but we might wanna do a sequel with that character and with Linda. We're very excited about Linda.

Hader’s animated version of The Cat in the Hat is much different than SNL because it isn’t a parody like his first run as the character was. It’s a more family-friendly retelling of the picture book with an expanded story about where The Cat comes from, and involves an imaginative plot line that’s perfect for the medium of animation. It hits theaters this Friday, November 6.

#3749. Remedy revenue soars by 226% following release of Control Resonant, the developer's fastest-selling game ever

Remedy - the developer behind the recently released Control Resonant - has released a scorcher of a quarterly financial report. It shows that following Resonant's release in September, the company's revenue surged by 226 percent, bringing in €39.6m in Q3.

This performance was described as "a defining milestone for the company" by CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon. The company reported a €0.6m operating profit this quarter, a fair leap upwards from the €16.4m loss from this time last year.

There are some interesting highlights to this sudden surging performance. For one, the US made up nearly half of Control Resonant's players across PC and console, followed by Chinese-speaking regions and then the UK.

Perhaps most crucially is that nearly half of Control Resonant's players were entirely new to the franchise, with the company stating: "Reaching new players was a key goal for this game, and these early results indicate a growing audience for the franchise and for Remedy."

Control (2019) also saw a bump up in sales thanks to the release of Control Resonant, showing a stronger performance this quarter than the past two quarters this year as well as its comparison period (this quarter last year).

Remedy's CEO now believes the focus for the studio is to "get Resonant into the hands of more players." He continues to say the game has provided a solid foundation for growth as other projects (including the Max Payne 1 & 2 remake) are in the works. In short, things appear to be looking rather good for Remedy.

Control Resonant was an artistically impressive but critically divisive game. While many praised the series' adventure into third person action, some felt it had less of a narrative bite than its predecessor. Nonetheless the game quickly blasted past one million sales after launch.

#3746. It looks like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 had fewer active players at launch in the US compared to last year's Black Ops 7

It's been speculated for a while that Call of Duty may be losing its lustre. Although we don't have concrete data with detailed statistics for each game released in the last several years, there's an observable trend in player numbers that's hard to ignore.

US market analysis firm Circana published some data showing player engagement with Modern Warfare 4 following its launch, and compared them to those by Black Ops 7.

The data is based on Circana's proprietary Player Engagement Tracker, which tracks player activity in the US across Steam and PlayStation, and worldwide on Xbox. According to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, 19 percent of players on PlayStation played Modern Warfare 4 in the week ending 24th October, compared to 17 percent on Xbox, and 4.2 percent on Steam.

With the exception of Steam, those numbers are down compared to last year's Black Ops 7, which saw 23 percent engagement on PlayStation, 29 percent on Xbox, and a meagre 1.5 percent on Steam during its launch week.

Call of Duty managed to land in the top 10 across all three platforms during the same week ending 24th October, per Circana. In fact, it sat just below Fortnite on PlayStation, which is a decent result.

The large drop in activity on Xbox could be explained by Modern Warfare 4's lack of a day-one release on Game Pass. Black Ops 7 was the second (and last) Call of Duty to launch on Game Pass day-and-date with its premium release. Game Pass availability typically boosts player numbers, though not always sales.

The drop on PlayStation is a little harder to explain, but could be a side effect of the incredibly successful Black Ops 1 & 2 ports released in the summer on PS4 and PS5, which captured lapsed players who may have simply lost interest in modern Call of Duty, regardless of the perceived quality of Modern Warfare 4.

Judging by the data we have access to, such as SteamDB numbers showing Modern Warfare 4's launch compared to Black Ops 7's and other recent releases, there's evidence this year's game perhaps isn't as popular as it could've been.

Indeed, even Activision's tenor when talking about Call of Duty first weekend sales has changed. The publisher issued a single statement following Modern Warfare 4's launch, through Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, which does not even mention the game by name.

"One of the most celebrated Call of Duty games in its 24-year history, and now $40bn in lifetime franchise revenue," Sharma wrote on X. "An incredible milestone. Congrats to the Activision team. And to the players, thank you for being with us."

Last year's Black Ops 7 post-launch statement sidestepped talk of sales and revenue entirely, insteading praising the "great response to the quality and depth of gameplay in Black Ops 7".

#3745. All Cloudreach Falls Aniimo locations

The Whisperwake Isles region has opened up in Aniimo, and by exploring this vast land, you can find and collect all kinds of new creatures. One of the areas you must traverse is Cloudreach Falls, which has quite a collection of Aniimo for you to find.

In each unique area you can explore, tracking down all of the Aniimo who call the region home can be tough, as they’ve all got only a few specific spawn locations, and many of them can only be found under special conditions. If you’re struggling to find any of these creatures, here are the locations of all Aniimo found around the Cloudfall Reach region in Aniimo.

In total, there are 14 unique Aniimo you can encounter around Cloudreach Falls. Some of them are exclusive to this region, while others can be found around a few different areas in Aniimo.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Each of the 14 Aniimo wandering around Cloudreach Falls has a few different habitat locations. Here’s exactly where to find all Cloudreach Falls Aniimo and a breakdown of any special conditions that must be met to get them.

Jeglid spawns at quite a few spots around Cloudreach Falls, including the upper middle region and the lower middle area, close to the teleport points in both areas. You can also find them around the lower eastern edge of this region.

You can find Jeglid (Tempest form) near the middle, upper right edge of Cloudreach Falls. This Aniimo only spawns during stormy weather, so you’ll have to wait and watch for this condition, or work to change the weather for it to spawn. It only spawns around the two spots marked below, making it fairly easy to spot once the conditions are right.

You can find Jeburst close to the water near the middle of Cloudreach Falls, east of the teleport point in this area. Jeburst also spawns a bit further south, near some water in this region.

Jeburst (Tempest form) can be found in the water pool at the bottom of the waterfall near the northeast end of this area. This Aniimo only spawns in stormy weather, though, so you must wait for these conditions to find and catch one.

Dewlop (Waterfall form) is pretty prevalent, with lots of different spawn regions around this area. This Aniimo is so common that you’re likely to run into it naturally while simply exploring. If not, though, you can visit any of the areas marked below to encounter them. They’re particularly abundant up north.

The Dewple (Waterfall form) is a bit of a special one, as it can only be found at one specific spot in the Cloudreach Falls area. To locate it, head to the spot marked below, find the large rock in the pool of water at this location, and use an Aniimo ability to destroy the rock. Jump into the water geyser that’s released upon breaking the rock, and capture the Dewple (Waterfall form) Aniimo once it appears in this stream.

You can find Saws swimming around a few different areas, including near the middle teleport point, close to the south end of the area, and on the small island a bit offshore. This Aniimo sticks to the water, so when searching for them, be sure to look in the water to find this species.

Whirlbite spawns around most of the same areas as Saws, and they also stick close to the water. You can go searching for them in the water pools up north, near the south end of Cloudreach Falls, and over on the small island off the coast.

To get Whirlbite (Prismana form), head to the Bloom marked on the map below. Nurture this Bloom frequently and catch all Aniimo that spawn around it. Eventually, you’ll increase the Prismana Flow state enough for Whirlbite (Prismana form) to spawn. When they do, you’ll get a special pop-up letting you know, and their location will be marked on the map.

You can find Eko in abundance around the northern end of Cloudreach Falls. Look all around the teleport point situated in the middle of this area to spot lots of them wandering around.

There are only two habitat spawn spots for Eklue. One is southwest of the middle teleport point and the other is northeast of it, close to the edge of the island. This Aniimo is fairly rare, so scan carefully to ensure you don’t miss it.

Ekrim can be found at three locations around Cloudreach Falls. One is located a bit east of the middle teleport point, and the other two are slightly south of it. This Aniimo is also quite rare, so there’s only one to be found at each spot.

You can find loads of Puffby roaming around the tall cliffs situated near the northwest end of Cloudreach Falls. They’re fairly common as long as you’re hunting for them in this area.

Hypnowls are by far the most abundant Aniimo in the Cloudreach Falls region. Of all the creatures you can find here, this is the one you’re likely going to run into the most, especially when exploring the lower southern part of this area.

If you’re looking for more to get done in Aniimo, consider working on some other tasks next, like finding Umbral Aniimo, checking out all Astra shops, vendors, games, and what they sell, and getting Sparkling Cubes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You may well be sick of reading about it—I am certainly sick to my stomach writing about it—but here's another doom-filled prophecy about the continuing memory crisis. Doesn't seem quite so funny calling it a RAMpocalypse now. The CEO of memory module maker TeamGroup, Chen Ching, is claiming we still haven't seen the worst of the supply crisis, and that even in 2027 "there will be no downward price trend whatsoever."

According to a report from BigGo Finance, which cropped up while I was searching for a credible source after mydrivers wrote about it, Chen thinks the worst of the shortage will be from now until the middle of next year, and that we're likely to get to a point with DRAM that "even money can't buy goods".

"Right now you can still buy goods, they're just expensive," he says. "In a little while, you may not be able to buy goods at all."

This is all on the back of an earnings call for the company, where it announced record quarterly revenue of NT$10.139 billion (around $308 million), which is an increase of 34% compared with last quarter.

TeamGroup, like most memory manufacturers looking to capitalise on the current crisis, is prioritising where it can get the most cash from, and that comes from selling direct to data centre and enterprise folk, rather than us normies. Just as chatty Sam Altman would like it to be. Fully two thirds of TeamGroup's business is now selling into other businesses, where previously that percentage was just a quarter, with the majority going into the consumer market.

Chen claims its relationships with vendors will help it continue to get inventory, even if it has to pay premium spot prices for it. But he notes that supply will continue to be the big problem, suggesting that supply and demand equilibrium is unlikely to be achieved any time before the second half of 2028, or potentially even later.

And, obviously, that means prices will remain high, or more likely keep rising. "How can prices fall when there's nothing left?" he questions like a good little doom-monger. Good 'ere, innit?
